chapter: Back in New York: Heard and Dizzy
title: Mid-1940s idols: Coleman Hawkins, Don Byas and Ben Webster
summary: He explains what he most admired in Hawkins, Don Byas and Ben Webster at the time.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: You know when we spoke earlier I asked you who were some of the earliest influences that you had and you mentioned people like Chu Berry and Herschel Evans and I wonder now, some years have gone by and you've established yourself in the big time, playin' with the big bands and I wonder at this point, say in the middle '40's, who you were most listening to, whose sound was most attractive to you?

Well Coleman Hawkins, mainly, because he seemed to have everything. All of his notes were clear and beautiful and he had an evenness about his horn and then his brain, he seemed to have such a deep knowledge of sound and chord structure and he just seemed to have everything. And he was actually cultural in his sound. And later on I found out that, you know, he played piano and played cello. And when I went to his home several times, then I realized that he had all the operas and all the scores and he played beautiful piano, as I said before, and this was the man, you know. And I liked Don Byas, because he was smooth; he had a

tremendous technique and he had a nice understanding of musical structure. And he had good time and he was just absolutely great. Now Ben Webster, his playing was...he had such a big gorgeous sound and he had such marvelous taste. His choice of notes was so attractive. And these three people I watched all the time.
